summary: Defines an EPP mapping for a key relay object that passes DNSSEC key material between EPP clients via the poll queue, so a domain's DNS operator can change without breaking the DNSSEC chain of trust.

plainLanguage.summary: When switching DNS providers, the old and new ones need to hand over a secret note safely. This gives them a standard way.

questions: how to change dns operator with dnssec
subtitle: How DNS operators hand DNSSEC keys to each other through the registry's EPP poll queue.

tldr.problem: When a domain moves to a new DNS operator, the old and new operators must exchange DNSSEC key material to keep the chain of trust intact, but often there is no trusted direct path between them.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends an EPP create command carrying a key relay object, and the registry places it on the poll queue of the registrar on record, acting only as a relay.
tldr.outcome: It defines a standard EPP extension for this exchange, as a Standards Track document. The registry does not complete the change itself; the losing DNS operator must act on the relayed keys.

facts.label: Revocation
facts.value: Past absolute date or zero period

today: RFC 8063 is a Standards Track document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Relay Keys Through the Registry
sections.content:
Some actions by a DNS operator need an authenticated exchange of information between DNS operators. Often there is no direct channel between them, or the direct channel does not scale and is insecure. One such action is exchanging DNSSEC key material when the DNS operator of a signed zone changes.

The RFC suggests that DNS operators use the administrative EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) channel to bootstrap the delegation by relaying the DNSSEC key material for the zone. It defines an EPP extension for sending that key material between EPP clients, so the transfer of a domain name can keep the DNSSEC chain of trust intact.
sections.plainLanguage: Two companies need to swap a secret code but do not trust the phone line between them. Both trust the same post office, so the code goes through it.

sections.title: The Registry as a Relay
sections.content:
DNS operators need to exchange DNSSEC key material before the registration data can be changed. The exchange is normally initiated through the gaining registrar. The gaining and losing DNS operators could talk directly to exchange the DNSKEY, but often there is no trusted path between the two. Both can securely interact with the registry over the administrative channel through the registrar, so the registry can act as a relay.

The registry is merely a relay channel. It is up to the losing DNS operator to complete the intended transaction. The registry SHOULD have policies requiring the losing DNS operator to cooperate, but that is beyond the scope of the document.

EPP itself makes no distinction between registrars and DNS operators; it only knows an EPP client and an EPP server, so the RFC uses the term EPP client.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk only passes the note along. It is up to the old babysitter to read it and do what it says.

sections.title: The Key Relay Data Element
sections.content:
The key material is carried in a <keyRelayData> element. It contains one REQUIRED <keyData> element holding the DNSSEC key material as described in RFC 5910, Section 4, and an OPTIONAL <expiry> element describing the expected lifetime of the relayed keys in the zone.

When <expiry> is given, the losing DNS operator SHOULD remove the inserted key material from the zone after the expiry time. A client that receives a key relay object it has seen before MUST update the expiry time, which lets clients extend the lifetime when a transfer is delayed.

<expiry> MUST contain exactly one of two children. <absolute> gives a date and time until which the keys are valid. <relative> gives a duration. A date in the past, or a period of zero, MUST be interpreted as a revocation of a previously sent key relay object.
sections.plainLanguage: The note holds the key and, if you like, a use-by time. A use-by time already passed means 'forget that key'.

sections.title: Create and Poll Commands
sections.content:
A client sends an EPP <create> command containing a <keyrelay:create> element. It has a REQUIRED <name> (the domain), a REQUIRED <authInfo> (authorization information for the domain object from RFC 5731), and one or more REQUIRED <keyRelayData> elements. When the command validates, the server MUST insert a poll message in the poll queue of the registrar on record for that domain.

The receiving client gets the object with the normal EPP <poll> command. The poll response's <resData> MUST contain a <keyrelay:infData> element with the same name, authInfo and key relay data, plus optional <crDate> (when the create was submitted), <reID> (the requesting client) and <acID> (the client that SHOULD act on it).

A server MAY limit how many <keyRelayData> elements it accepts. If that policy is violated, or if the server knows the receiving client does not support key relay, it MUST answer with EPP result code 2308 "Data management policy violation". The commands <check>, <info>, <transfer>, <delete>, <renew> and <update> have no mapping for key relay objects.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand the front desk a sealed note with the house name and a password. The desk drops it into the other person's mailbox, and they pick it up the next time they check.

sections.title: Formal Syntax and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC gives an XML schema for the extension with elements keyRelayData, infData and create. The expiry type is a choice between an absolute dateTime and a relative duration.

IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:keyrelay-1.0, the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:keyrelay-1.0, and the extension in the EPP extension registry with status Active.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for what the note must look like are written down, and the official list of such notes now includes this one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A server SHOULD NOT transform data under server management when processing a <keyrelay:create> command, because the intent is to put the key material on another client's poll queue. Exceptions are allowed only for interoperability with server policies that already implemented the extension.

Any EPP client can use the mechanism to put data on another client's message queue, which allows a potential denial-of-service attack. The server should detect this and MAY limit or reject <keyrelay:create> commands if it sees abuse.

A correct <domain:authInfo> is the indication that the domain's registrant authorized putting the key material on the receiving client's queue. Which clients may change DNS is registry policy and not covered. A sender can check in DNS that the key was added to the authoritative zone, which shows the key arrived end to end, but says nothing about the chain of trust.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone could try to stuff someone's mailbox, so the desk can stop troublemakers. The password shows the house owner said yes.
